title: How We Got Here: A History of Christian Nationalism in America
subtitle: From a Puritan sermon to a modern rallying cry, the long story of how the faith kept getting recruited to bless the nation, and the one distinction that tells worship from idolatry.

sections.title: The Covenant and the City
sections.body:
The story does not begin in a political party. It begins in a sermon on the water. In 1630, aboard the ship carrying the first great wave of Puritans to Massachusetts, John Winthrop told his people they would be as a city upon a hill, the eyes of all the world upon them, bound to God in a covenant like the one at Sinai. If they kept faith, they would be blessed. If they broke it, they would be a byword and a curse. New England was not to be merely a colony. It was to be a new Israel, a people chosen and watched.

Take the theology seriously before judging it, because Winthrop meant something humbling by it. A covenant is a two-edged thing. To be chosen was chiefly to be accountable, held to a higher standard, exposed to a sharper judgment. The Puritans trembled at the arrangement as often as they boasted of it. This was not yet nationalism. It was a demanding, self-suspecting faith that happened to imagine an ocean crossing as an errand from God.

But an idea can be handed down while its humility is quietly dropped. The seed planted on that deck was the conviction that this land stands in a special relationship to God, chosen among the nations for a purpose. Later generations would keep the chosenness and lose the trembling. They would keep the city on the hill and forget that Winthrop's whole point was that the watching world would see them fail if they turned from justice and mercy to greed. The covenant was built to accuse its own people first. What survived was the flattery. What died was the warning. That exchange, made over and over across four centuries, is the history of Christian nationalism in one sentence.

sections.title: Providence and the Continent
sections.body:
When the colonies broke from Britain, the pulpits went to war first. Ministers framed the Revolution as a providential act, the colonies cast as a new Israel fleeing a new Pharaoh, liberty baptized as a sacred and God-given cause. The men at the top were often cooler than that, Deists and rationalists as much as churchmen, but the people were moved in the idiom of Scripture, and the war was preached as much as it was fought. The nation was born wrapped in providence.

Then providence acquired a map. In 1845 the journalist John O'Sullivan, arguing first for the annexation of Texas and then for a claim to Oregon, wrote that it was the nation's manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence. The phrase caught because it named something many Americans already felt, that the westward taking of a continent was not conquest but calling, ordained by God. The covenant had become a deed to real estate.

Follow that idea to its fruit and stop pretending it was harmless. Manifest destiny sanctified the removal and destruction of native peoples and a war of expansion against Mexico, and it did so with Scripture in its mouth. This is the pattern already turning. The Puritan hoped to be found worthy of a calling. The expansionist assumed the calling and used it to bless whatever he had already resolved to take. When a nation decides in advance that God is on its side, the question of whether it is on God's side stops being asked. That is not faith moving into public life. That is public appetite dressing itself in faith.

sections.title: Both Armies Prayed
sections.body:
The Civil War is where the whole confusion becomes impossible to hide, because both sides prayed to the same God and both were sure He was theirs. The Confederacy wrote its dependence on Almighty God into its constitution and preached secession as a holy cause. The Union sang of the coming glory of the Lord and of the trampling out of the vintage where the grapes of wrath are stored. Northern and Southern pulpits alike proved from the same Bible that their war was righteous, and Mark Noll has called this the theological crisis of the war, that a nation drenched in Scripture could not use Scripture to settle the one question tearing it apart.

Into that certainty on both sides came one voice that refused it. In his Second Inaugural in March of 1865, with victory in sight and every reason to claim God for the North, Abraham Lincoln said instead that both read the same Bible and pray to the same God, and each invokes His aid against the other. He would not hand God to his own cause. He put the whole nation, North included, under a judgment neither side controlled. It remains the greatest sentence any American ever spoke about God and country, and it is the exact opposite of nationalism.

Then the war ended and the losing side sacralized its defeat. The Lost Cause remade the Confederacy into a holy and martyred civilization, its generals into saints, its war into a noble crusade, and it fused that myth with the church across the South. Charles Reagan Wilson documented how thoroughly the religion of the Lost Cause baptized white supremacy and called it faithfulness. The pattern holds and darkens. God is claimed. The claim serves the thing the claimant already loved.

sections.title: One Nation Under God
sections.body:
Much of what feels like timeless Christian America was actually built in the 1950s, and knowing that should change how the argument sounds. After the Second World War, with the country locked against an officially atheist Soviet Union, being American and being religious fused into a single posture, faith as the thing that separated the free world from the godless one. Congress inserted the words 'under God' into the Pledge of Allegiance in 1954. Two years later, in 1956, it made 'In God We Trust' the official national motto. These are not ancient inheritances. They are younger than living memory.

The historian Kevin Kruse has shown that this fusion did not rise on its own from the pews. It was organized, promoted through the 1930s and 1940s by business leaders and clergy who wove piety, patriotism, and free enterprise into one creed, and it reached full flower under a president who spoke easily of an America defined by faith. The revival of the fifties was real, but so was the machinery behind its public symbols.

Here honesty has to cut against the reflex to sneer. That generation was not merely cynical. Many meant every word, and the contrast with Soviet tyranny was not imaginary. But a faith recruited to certify a nation against its enemies has already begun to change jobs. It is no longer mainly worshipping God. It is mainly defining us, marking the boundary between the real Americans and the suspect ones. The Cold War did not invent that move. It simply handed the old covenant idea a flag, an enemy, and a slogan stamped on the money.

sections.title: The Moral Majority
sections.body:
The version we argue about now took its shape in 1979, when Jerry Falwell founded the Moral Majority and turned a diffuse religious unease into a voting bloc. The trigger was not a single issue but a sense that the culture had slipped its moorings, and the answer offered was political organization at scale, registering the faithful, rating the candidates, delivering the votes. In 1980 that machine helped elect Ronald Reagan, who told a gathering of religious conservatives that they could not endorse him but he endorsed them, and the marriage of a religious movement to a political party was sealed.

Something changed in that fusion that is easy to miss. A religious identity became a partisan identity, until over the following decades the question of which church you attended predicted which party you supported more reliably than almost anything else. Faith did not merely inform politics. The two began to trade places, and for many the political loyalty became the load-bearing one, the faith increasingly its chaplain.

That is the road to the present, where the phrase 'Christian nation' has come roaring back as a rallying cry and a growing number openly argue that the country should be governed as one. The history should make us slower and sadder about this, not more partisan. What looks like a return to the founding is mostly the latest turn of a much older habit, the covenant nation dreaming its dream again. Every generation that reached for it believed it was defending the faith. Every generation discovered, too late, that it had recruited the faith to defend something else.

sections.title: Civil Religion and Its Counterfeit
sections.body:
So name precisely what we have been watching. In 1967 the sociologist Robert Bellah argued that America has always carried a civil religion, a set of shared symbols invoking a general God, distinct from any church. Bellah did not think this was simply a disease. At its best it had a prophetic edge, calling the nation to account before a God who stood above it. Lincoln at his Second Inaugural was its high priest, and a century later so was Martin Luther King, summoning America to its own creed under a judgment it did not control.

That is the distinction that matters. Philip Gorski calls one strand a prophetic civil religion, which puts the nation under God, and the other religious nationalism, which puts God under the nation. The first says we will be judged by whether we do justice. The second says God is ours and blesses what we have already chosen. King stood in the first. The Lost Cause stood in the second. They are not two degrees of one thing. They are opposites that happen to use the same words.

And here I have to turn it on my own tribe, because the counterfeit is not housed in one party. The right builds it out of the founding and the flag. The left builds it out of the movement and the cause, translating the kingdom of God into a policy platform and enlisting Jesus as its campaign. Same idol, other altar. The test is simple, and it indicts everyone. Does your God ever tell your side no. If He only ever blesses what you already wanted, you are not worshipping God. You are worshipping your own reflection and calling it faith. The nation is not the church. It never was. The day we forget the difference, we lose the one thing that could have saved the nation, a church that still answered to someone above it.
